e-8256.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable
e-8256.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} 
= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =[-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot 1+[-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})-t{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}) \\  & =-(1+t){e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

e-8257.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
e-8257.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-8258.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables
e-8258.problem: Let $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2,$ where $x = s\cos{t}$ and $y = t\sin{s}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
e-8258.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s)(\operatorname{sin}⁡s) \\  & =-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t{sin}^{2}⁡s \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the identity $\sin 2t = 2\sin t\cos t$ in the above simplification.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ln⁡y,∂f∂y=1+xy

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=ln⁡2s,∂f∂y=1+s2s=32.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=1,dyds=2.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=ln⁡2s⋅1+32⋅2=3+ln⁡2s.

\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=ex+2y,x=s2, and y=s, compute dfds.

a
2ses2+2s
b
2(s+1)es2+2s
c
s(s+2)es2+2s
d
s2es2+2s
e
2(s+2)es2+2s
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(s)=e^{s^2+2s}. By the chain rule, df/ds=(2s+2)e^{s^2+2s}=2(s+1)e^{s^2+2s}.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+2y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 2s+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 1 \\  & =2s{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s} \\  & =2(s+1){e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=ex+2y,x=s2, and y=s, compute dfds.

a
2ses2+2s
b
2(s+1)es2+2s
c
s(s+2)es2+2s
d
s2es2+2s
e
2(s+2)es2+2s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ex+2y,∂f∂y=2ex+2y

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=es2+2s,∂f∂y=2es2+2s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=2s,dyds=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=es2+2s⋅2s+2es2+2s⋅1=2ses2+2s+2es2+2s=2(s+1)es2+2s.

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution declares 2(s+1)e^{s^2+2s}, matching option b. Independently, differentiating e^{s^2+2s} gives (2s+2)e^{s^2+2s}, confirming that result.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+2y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 2s+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 1 \\  & =2s{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s} \\  & =2(s+1){e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-{e}^{2y-x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{2y-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =-{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t){e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

a

b
(2sin⁡tcos⁡t+1)e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t
c
e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t

EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=−e2y−x,∂f∂y=2e2y−x

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=−e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t,∂f∂y=2e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=−sin⁡t,dydt=cos⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=−e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+2e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t⋅cos⁡t=(sin⁡t+2cos⁡t)e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

If f(x,y)=yex, x=s and y=s, compute dfds for s>0.

a
(1+s)es
b
(1+s2)es
c
(2+s)es
d
(1+1s)es
e
(1+12s)es
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(s)=s e^{√s}. The product and chain rules give df/ds=e^{√s}+s e^{√s}/(2√s)=(1+√s/2)e^{√s}, matching option b.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}}+{e}^{\sqrt{s}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}{e}^{\sqrt{s}}+{e}^{\sqrt{s}} \\  & =(1+\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}){e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

If f(x,y)=yex, x=s and y=s, compute dfds for s>0.

a
(1+s)es
b
(1+s2)es
c
(2+s)es
d
(1+1s)es
e
(1+12s)es
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=yex,∂f∂y=ex

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=ses,∂f∂y=es.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=12s,dyds=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=ses⋅12s+es⋅1=s2es+es=(1+s2)es.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}}+{e}^{\sqrt{s}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}{e}^{\sqrt{s}}+{e}^{\sqrt{s}} \\  & =(1+\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}){e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot 2x \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

If f(x,y)=sin⁡(x2+y) and y=x2, compute dfdx.

a
(x2+1)cos⁡(x2)
b
4xcos⁡(2x2)
c
2x(x+1)sin⁡(x2)
d
2xsin2⁡(2x)
e
2x3cos⁡(2x2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xcos⁡(x2+y),∂f∂y=cos⁡(x2+y)

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=2xcos⁡(x2+x2)=2xcos⁡(2x2),∂f∂y=cos⁡(x2+x2)=cos⁡(2x2).

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=2x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=2xcos⁡(2x2)+cos⁡(2x2)⋅2x=2xcos⁡(2x2)+2xcos⁡(2x2)=4xcos⁡(2x2).

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+{x}^{2})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot 2x \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x+2{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x(1+2x)}{x(1+x)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{1+2x}{1+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x+2{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x(1+2x)}{x(1+x)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{1+2x}{1+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 8
?

If f(x,y)=yx+1 and y=x3, compute dfdx.

a
x(3x+4)(x+1)2
b
x(4x−3)x+1
c
4x2(x−6)x+1
d
x2(3x2−1)(x+1)2
e
x2(2x+3)(x+1)2
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x³ gives f(x)=x³/(x+1). The quotient rule gives df/dx=[3x²(x+1)-x³]/(x+1)²=x²(2x+3)/(x+1)², matching option e.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

If f(x,y)=yx+1 and y=x3, compute dfdx.

a
x(3x+4)(x+1)2
b
x(4x−3)x+1
c
4x2(x−6)x+1
d
x2(3x2−1)(x+1)2
e
x2(2x+3)(x+1)2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−y(x+1)2,∂f∂y=1x+1

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=−x3(x+1)2,∂f∂y=1x+1.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=3x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=−x3(x+1)2+1x+1⋅3x2=3x2x+1−x3(x+1)2=3x2(x+1)−x3(x+1)2=3x3+3x2−x3(x+1)2=x2(2x+3)(x+1)2.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

If f(x,y)=cos⁡(x2+y) and y=1x, compute dfdx.

a
(1−3x3)sin⁡(x2+1x2)
b
(2x2+1x)sin⁡(x3+1x)
c
(1−4x3x)cos⁡(x3+1x2)
d
(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x)
e
(1+4x2)cos⁡(x2−1x)
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting y=1/x gives f(x)=cos(x²+1/x). Its derivative is -(2x-1/x²)sin(x²+1/x)=[(1-2x³)/x²]sin((x³+1)/x), matching option d.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

If f(x,y)=cos⁡(x2+y) and y=1x, compute dfdx.

a
(1−3x3)sin⁡(x2+1x2)
b
(2x2+1x)sin⁡(x3+1x)
c
(1−4x3x)cos⁡(x3+1x2)
d
(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x)
e
(1+4x2)cos⁡(x2−1x)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+y),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+y)

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+1x).

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=−1x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x)+(−sin⁡(x2+1x))⋅(−1x2)=(1x2−2x)sin⁡(x2+1x)=(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x).

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(1+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

If f(x,y)=xey and y=sin⁡x, compute dfdx.

a
esin⁡x(1+xcos⁡x)
b
esin⁡x(1−cos⁡x)
c
esin⁡x(1+xsin⁡x)
d
ecos⁡x(1−xsin⁡x)
e
ecos⁡x(1+sin⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ey,∂f∂y=xey

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=esin⁡x,∂f∂y=xesin⁡x.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=cos⁡x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=esin⁡x+xesin⁡x⋅cos⁡x=esin⁡x(1+xcos⁡x).

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(1+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$
